courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Why radiance fields needed a rasterizer instead of ray marching
md: 3DGS keeps NeRF's blending formula but replaces the implicit neural field with explicit primitives. Explicit primitives can be projected and rasterized, so rendering cost scales with the number of splats that touch a pixel, not with hundreds of network queries per ray.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: LL/SC: watching the location instead of its value
md: Portable C and C++ code does not get LL/SC semantics. `compare_exchange` is defined as a value comparison; on an LL/SC machine the compiler builds it from an LL/SC loop that starts *after* your earlier plain load of `top`. The window where ABA strikes (between that load and the CAS) is outside the reservation, so ABA is back.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Interaction effects and Shapley values
md: Shapley values are a summary, not a full account. They need $v$ for all $2^n$ configurations (16 here; for many components, sampled orders are the usual approximation). They hide that P is harmful without R, and they average over queries. Report the interaction cells and per-query spread too.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: Reading a leaderboard: harness, noise, cost and contamination
md: Checklist for any agent leaderboard number: which subset and version; which harness, tools, step and cost budget; one attempt or best of many (pass@k vs pass^1 vs pass^k); how many tasks and trials, with an interval; and whether the tasks predate the model's training cutoff.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Why an agent cannot just replay its whole history
md: A memory system is defined by four decisions: what to write, how to reconcile it with what is already stored, what to retrieve for a given step, and what to forget. Retrieval alone is RAG; the write and forget decisions are what make it memory.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Best-of-N with an imperfect verifier: the accuracy ceiling
md: FPR sets the ceiling, TPR sets the speed. With enough samples, best-of-N accuracy converges to the verifier's precision $pt / (pt + (1-p)f)$. Raising TPR only means you need fewer samples to get there.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Stability: formation energy and energy above the convex hull
md: The hull test is a 0 K, zero-pressure, ordered-crystal calculation (the Materials Project docs state the 0 K, 0 atm assumption). It ignores entropy, so it can favor artificially ordered arrangements of similar atoms that would be disordered at real synthesis temperatures. "On the hull" means "thermodynamically plausible in DFT", not "can be made in a lab".

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Detection is a z-test on the green count
md: A tiny false positive rate is not zero at scale. $z > 4$ means a one-sided p of $3.2 \times 10^{-5}$: scan a million human documents and expect about 32 false flags. Hugging Face's `WatermarkDetector` defaults to $z > 3$, where the rate is $1.3 \times 10^{-3}$. Pick the threshold for the cost of a false accusation.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Replaying workloads to compare allocators
md: Workflow: capture once with an interposer, analyze with a heap profiler to find what to fix in code, convert to a workload, then replay that one workload against each allocator or tuning and compare RSS against ideal RSS.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Anomalies in time: seasonal baselines and robust residuals
md: For time series, first remove what is predictable (seasonality and level), then apply a robust score to the residual. The detector is only as good as the baseline: a residual is anomalous relative to a model of normal for that moment.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
md: Tuning tradeoffs follow directly from the passes. Rare checkpoints and slow background page writes make the smallest recLSN old, so redo scans more log. Long-running transactions make undo long and keep old log needed. Frequent checkpoints shorten redo but cost extra log and page writes at runtime.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
md: A semaphore limits **how many** requests are in flight, not **how fast** they start. Concurrency times the inverse of latency gives your request rate, so when latency drops (short prompts, cache hits) the same semaphore sends requests faster. Pair it with a rate limiter, covered next.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
md: The budget only helps tasks that keep awaiting **Tokio** resources. It cannot interrupt a tight CPU loop or a blocking call, and the Tokio team has said it will not detect blocked workers and add threads automatically. Fixing those is your job.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: A pretrained audio model never sees a whole clip at once. It sees fixed 0.96 s log-mel patches and returns one embedding and one score vector per patch. Everything about clip-level decisions (lesson 3) is about combining those per-patch outputs.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tracking sources and checking every citation
md: A citation that exists is not a citation that supports. Checking that every URL resolves catches invented sources but misses the more common failure: a real page cited for a claim it does not make.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Below the API: Inferentia, Trainium, Neuron and SageMaker AI
md: Moving work onto Inferentia or Trainium is a **compiler** project as much as a hardware choice: your model must compile with Neuron, and custom ops may need NKI kernels. Budget engineering time for that, not just instance price.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Why a pipelined CPU has to guess at every branch
md: Speculation is not a correctness risk for your program: wrong-path results never reach registers or memory. It is only a time cost. (It can leak information through caches, which is the Spectre family of attacks; lesson 5 touches on that.)

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables
md: LSM reads search from newest to oldest and stop at the first entry for the key, whether that is a value or a tombstone. Correctness depends only on this ordering, never on old versions being gone.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU, CLOCK and PostgreSQL clock-sweep on a 4-frame pool
md: CLOCK is not "LRU but cheaper" in every case. It only approximates recency, and when all bits are set it evicts in plain circular order. Its win is that a hit costs one bit or counter update with no shared list to reorder.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Entropy patching: spend compute where the next byte is hard
md: Entropy patching spends a global step where the next byte is hard to predict and lets cheap local layers handle predictable runs. The threshold sets the average patch size, and therefore the compute.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Safe wrappers over unsafe code: split_at_mut and soundness
md: Audit unsafe code at the module boundary. Keep fields that unsafe code trusts private, check every invariant before the unsafe block (as `assert!(mid <= len)` does), and write a SAFETY comment that names the invariant.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Where a line may live: sets, ways and tags
md: Capacity is set by size, conflicts by associativity and address bits. A bigger cache fixes capacity misses; more ways or a less regular stride fixes conflict misses; nothing but prefetching hides cold misses.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Limitations, and tracing circuits yourself
md: An attribution graph explains one prompt in one replacement model. It is not proof of a general algorithm, it is silent about attention's choices, and any path through error nodes is unexplained. State those limits whenever you report a circuit.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Why CLIP learns from captions instead of fixed labels
md: CLIP does not learn to describe images. It learns two encoders whose outputs agree: a matching image and caption land close together in one shared vector space, and non-matching ones land apart. Everything else in this course (zero-shot classification, retrieval, the failure modes) follows from that geometry.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Three criteria, three answers on the same ten points: the elbow is ambiguous, VRC says k = 5, silhouette says k = 3. That disagreement is the lesson. Schubert's advice is to use a baseline-aware criterion (VRC, BIC or the gap statistic) rather than an elbow, and to spend your effort on preprocessing, "because garbage in, garbage out".

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Inside a vectorized pipeline: primitives and selection vectors
md: Vectorized engines split work into type-specialized primitives over arrays, and pass filters along as lists of positions instead of moving data.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
md: Without LTO, a .c file is the optimizer's horizon. LTO stores the compiler's IR in the object files and optimizes the whole program at link time. ThinLTO does the global analysis on small summaries and the heavy work in parallel, so it scales and supports incremental builds.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Misconception: a system prompt saying "ignore instructions on web pages" solves injection. It helps, but the model reads that prompt and the attacker's text through the same channel. Defenses that do not depend on the model obeying (no secrets in the VM, network allowlists, harness-enforced confirmations) are what hold when the model is fooled.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: ThreadSanitizer: catching races with vector clocks at runtime
md: TSan only sees code paths that actually run (the manual: it cannot find races in code paths that are not executed). And if, in this particular run, the two threads happened to pass through some unrelated lock in between, that lock creates a happens-before edge and hides the race. Coverage and varied workloads still matter.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Linearizability: one copy, respecting real time
md: A read that overlaps a write may return either the old or the new value. Once any read has returned the new value and completed, every later-starting read must return it too. Linearizability forbids the value from flickering back.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Hot keys: perfect key balance, unbalanced traffic
md: Splitting or replicating every key is wasteful: reads fan out or memory multiplies. Detect the few hot keys (sampling, per-key counters, top-k sketches) and treat only them specially. Facebook replicates only when a key family is small, fetched in big batches, and requested faster than one server can serve.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Why scheduling explodes, and what a constraint model is
md: A constraint solver separates **what** a solution is (the model) from **how** to find it (the search). You declare variables, domains and constraints; the solver chooses the order of guesses and the deductions. Adding a rule means adding one constraint, not rewriting a search loop.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: What an image actually is: layers, unions and digests
md: An image is an ordered list of content-addressed changesets plus a config. Everything else follows from that one sentence: identical layers are stored and transferred once, a deletion only adds a marker, and changing any layer invalidates every layer after it. Order your build steps from least to most frequently changing.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: References point at a response, not at the conversation. Store the ordered ids you displayed, with a version, and resolve ordinals, attributes and *those* against that stored list.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: CoT monitors, and what training against them does
md: Misconception: "the monitor flags less often after training, so the model behaves better." A falling flag rate is what both genuine improvement and obfuscation look like. Without an independent ground-truth check of the behavior, you cannot tell them apart.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
md: A larger max_length is not free and not always possible. Position embeddings fix the hard limit at training time (512 for BERT), and compute per pair grows with sequence length. For long documents, chunk and take the max (or another aggregate) instead of hoping truncation keeps the right part.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function
md: A layout is just a function: coordinate in, integer offset out, computed as an inner product with the strides. Everything else in CuTe (tiling, partitioning across threads, MMA operand maps) is built by combining such functions.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: The CUTLASS 3.x API, epilogues and tuning tradeoffs
md: A tile that maximizes arithmetic intensity can still lose: it may leave a tail wave, spill registers, or leave too little shared memory for stages. Measure with the CUTLASS profiler across candidate configurations rather than trusting one formula.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Why the pretraining mixture is a decision you cannot skip
md: The mixture is a vector of $k$ probabilities chosen **before** training, and it silently allocates billions of tokens. DoReMi's question: can we choose it automatically, cheaply, and without looking at downstream benchmarks?

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: Memory moves in cache lines. Lay out data so that the bytes a hot loop needs are packed together, and the bytes it skips live somewhere else.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels
md: A fixed seed proves nothing about kernel determinism, and batch-invariant kernels prove nothing about the sampler. Run two separate experiments: hold the batch fixed and vary the seed to test sampling, and hold the seed fixed while varying batch size and position to test the kernels. A test that varies both at once cannot attribute a failure.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
md: A masked diffusion LM is not just BERT. BERT masks a fixed 15% of tokens and has no way to sample a whole text. A masked diffusion LM trains on every masking ratio from 0 to 1 with a loss that bounds the likelihood, which is exactly what makes generation from an all-mask sequence possible.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
md: Goodput is not throughput. A colocated GPU at 4 req/s still produces plenty of tokens per second, but in the toy run only 29% of requests meet both SLOs. If you only tracked throughput, that overloaded point would look like the best one.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
md: Beam width W trades round trips for wasted reads; search list L trades reads for recall. Tune L for the recall target first, then pick the smallest W that meets the latency target, watching total reads against the SSD's IOPS budget.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: Turning a pair into one desirable and one undesirable example, as the paper does to compare against DPO, is described by its authors as a naive assumption: a chosen answer is only better than its sibling, not necessarily good.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Not every mismatch is a bug in the new store. If the new store is fed asynchronously, from a queue or a CDC stream, it is eventually consistent with the old one: a read right after a write can compare a fresh control with a candidate that is milliseconds behind. Measure that lag, and only `ignore` such cases after confirming they converge.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Common misconception: "eBPF is safe, so tracing can't hurt production." The verifier guarantees the kernel won't crash or hang, but it does not bound *how often* your program runs. A kprobe on a function called millions of times per second can still cost a large fraction of every CPU.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away
md: Cutting after the first correct answer is the most aggressive compression, and it costs accuracy on hard problems. The useful target is 'one solve plus one check', not 'one solve'.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
md: Event-based methods need step changes. Hart's own NALM page lists three appliance classes: ON/OFF (bulbs, toasters), multi-state (washing machines, dishwashers with fill, rinse and spin states) and continuously variable (light dimmers, variable-speed tools). The last class is hard to monitor nonintrusively because it does not generate step changes in power.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: The independence assumption double-counts correlated fields. Company name and website domain usually agree or disagree together, so adding both full weights overstates the evidence. Merge strongly correlated fields into one comparison, or check calibration on labeled pairs.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Draining one busy descriptor to `EAGAIN` can starve the others, since a fast sender may never let the buffer empty. epoll(7) suggests keeping your own ready list: mark the connection ready, process a bounded chunk, and round-robin across all ready connections before waiting again.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
md: A confidence interval or significance test computed on the same queries you used to pick the winner is not valid. Report CIs from a set that played no part in the choice.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Putting a price on the ping-pong
md: Simplified model: real chips overlap work with store buffers and out-of-order execution, prefetch, and have varying transfer latency by core distance. Use the model for direction and scaling, and measure the actual number on your hardware.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Stragglers, partial participation and the round quorum
md: A federated round is a **rendezvous with a quorum**, not a barrier over all clients. The server waits for a minimum percentage of a goal count within a time window, aggregates whoever made it, ignores the stragglers, and abandons the round if too few arrive.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Fine-grained experts: split each expert into m slices
md: Finer is not free forever. Each expert becomes a smaller matrix multiply, which uses the GPU less efficiently. DeepSeekMoE 16B stopped at experts one quarter the size of a standard FFN, citing the potential loss of computational efficiency from excessively small experts. DeepSeek-V3 uses 256 routed experts with an intermediate width of 2048.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine
md: Attention in serving is mostly about **memory traffic under irregular shapes**. FlashInfer's answer is to separate what is static (variant, layout, tile sizes: compile time) from what is dynamic (lengths, page lists: a cheap per-step plan).

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps
md: Sampling cost is set by how curved the learned paths are. A perfectly straight, constant-speed flow is solved exactly by one Euler step.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
md: The scale is a full-precision real number kept outside the FP8 data (in FP32), not a change to the format's exponent bias. The FP8 paper chose this deliberately: a software scale can take any value, while a programmable bias could only shift by powers of two.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Group commit: one WAL flush makes many transactions durable
md: Group commit does not make any single commit faster. With one client there is nothing to share and latency is one full flush. It raises **throughput** when many sessions commit concurrently, and it keeps latency from exploding as they queue.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
md: Lucene's javadoc documents a surprise: `FuzzyQuery` on `abcd` with `maxEdits=2` does not match the indexed term `ab`, even though the Levenshtein distance is 2. Engines add rules of their own on top of the textbook distance, so test short terms and other edge cases directly.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
md: A match is not the end product. The solver turns matched star pairs into CRPIX, CRVAL and a CD matrix under a TAN projection, which any FITS tool can then use to label every pixel with RA and Dec.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Resize: the half-pixel center, worked on a four-pixel row
md: A common misconception is that interpolation conventions only matter for image quality. They also move geometry. If training resized with half-pixel centers and inference resizes without them, every pixel coordinate the model predicts is offset by $(s-1)/2$ source pixels, and no amount of retraining the head fixes a preprocessing mismatch.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Streams: when a freed block is safe to reuse
md: Forgetting record_stream (or a wait_stream before the free) is a silent data race, not a crash: the new tensor's kernel on s0 may overwrite memory that s1 is still reading. The PyTorch docs note the synchronization is needed even when the side stream only writes.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Misalignment, strides and effective bandwidth
md: **Misconception:** the L1 cache makes access patterns irrelevant. Caches help when nearby warps reuse what was over-fetched, as with small misalignments. A large stride over data read once gets no reuse, and every unused byte still crosses the DRAM interface.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
md: Occupancy is a capability, not an achievement. 100 percent occupancy with 5 percent of peak throughput is a latency-bound kernel with plenty of warps and nothing for them to do, and the fix has nothing to do with occupancy.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Occupancy: how many warps fit on an SM at once
md: Higher occupancy is not automatically faster. Low occupancy hurts latency hiding, but past some point extra warps add nothing, and a lower-occupancy kernel can keep more data in registers and avoid spilling. Measure.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
md: Global search never retrieves by similarity. It asks every community at one level, lets the LLM score how useful each partial answer is, and keeps the best points. That is what makes it work for questions that look like nothing in the corpus.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Group-relative advantages: the baseline from sibling answers
md: In GRPO a sample's advantage means "how much better than its siblings on the same question". If all siblings agree (all right or all wrong), there is nothing to learn from that question.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Joining realtime to the schedule and propagating delay
md: Prediction at a stop = scheduled instant + the delay from the nearest StopTimeUpdate at or before it, unless that update is NO_DATA. SKIPPED stops are passed through, earlier stops are never filled in, and an absolute time beats a delay.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: Huge pages pay off three ways: one TLB entry covers 512 (or 262,144) times more memory, each miss walks fewer levels, and the page tables shrink. The kernel's THP doc calls the fourth effect, one page fault per 2 MiB instead of 512, almost irrelevant because it only happens on first touch.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: Pure SSMs are not simply worse. In the same NVIDIA study, Mamba-2 trained on 3.5T tokens beat the matching Transformer on average across standard zero-shot tasks. The gap is specific: copying, in-context learning and exact retrieval from the prompt.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Why a raw query is a poor probe for an unsupervised encoder
md: Short queries and long documents look different. A label-free encoder knows what *documents* resemble each other, but nobody taught it what *answers a question*. HyDE's trick is to stop comparing a question with answers at all.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu turns threshold selection into a 1D search over the histogram: maximize $\omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0-\mu_1)^2$. It works well when changed and unchanged pixels form two separated groups, and only then.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: SQPOLL is not a free "go faster" switch. The poll thread consumes a CPU while it spins. io_uring_sqpoll(7) warns it can hurt low-IOPS, bursty or CPU-bound workloads and that it only speeds up submission, not completion handling. Benchmark with and without it.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Why a healthy cluster hides consistency bugs
md: Jepsen judges a system only by its history: what clients asked for and what they were told. A violation is reported only when **no** legal execution of the claimed model could explain that history, so a failure is a real bug, not a guess.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Why the winner changes when the shape changes
md: A common bug is a tuning cache keyed on the kernel name alone, or on batch size only. It never misses, so it never re-tunes, and it silently serves a configuration chosen for a different shape. The symptom is a kernel that is fast in the benchmark that tuned it and mediocre everywhere else.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread
md: Measure with the right tool. SPDK reports up to 2.6 times more IOPS per core using its own `perf` tool than using fio with the SPDK plugin for 4 KiB random reads, because fio's flexibility costs cycles. A slow benchmark harness can hide a fast driver.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
md: The teacher's knowledge is its input-to-output mapping, including how much probability it gives to each wrong answer. Distillation transfers that mapping by using the teacher's full output distribution as the training target.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: KV bytes scale with layers x KV heads x head size x bytes per value x tokens x batch. Weights are paid once; the cache is paid per token per request, so at long context and large batch it dominates.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Eviction trades exactness for a fixed memory budget. Keep the sink tokens, keep recent tokens, and use accumulated attention to keep the heavy hitters; anything evicted cannot be recovered.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: A cached block after a gap is useless for this request. KV at position 7 depends on every earlier token through attention in every layer, so if block 6 must be recomputed, block 7 must be too, even if an identical hash for it were stored. Eviction that removes a middle block silently strands everything after it.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
md: HLC is still one-way like Lamport: $(l, c)$ ordering never tells you two events are concurrent. Its gain is closeness to real time and constant size, not concurrency detection.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
md: Late interaction is not free accuracy. You pay in index size, in memory bandwidth at query time, and in engine support. For large text corpora a common design is a cheap first stage (BM25 or a single-vector index) with ColBERT or ColPali scoring a few hundred candidates.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes
md: A continuous thought can encode a weighted set of next steps. Deferring commitment is what let Coconut reach 97.0% on ProsQA where CoT reached 77.5%, while generating 14.2 tokens instead of 49.4.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
md: Bounded search costs the leaf's worst-case error on every lookup. Exponential search costs the error of this lookup. Tight models favour bounded search; loose models with mostly good predictions favour exponential search.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Why ranking needs its own loss function
md: Ranking metrics depend on the scores only through the **sort**. Learning to rank works around that either by optimizing a smooth stand-in loss (RankNet, ListNet) or, in LambdaRank and LambdaMART, by writing down the gradient we want directly.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is not a cheap approximation of softmax attention that converges to it. The exponential kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature map (Katharopoulos et al.), so any finite state is a different, weaker model. That gap is what the rest of this course is about.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: From labels to leaderboards: do system rankings survive?
md: Label-level agreement can be modest (kappa 0.3 to 0.6) while system-level agreement is high (tau near 0.9), because errors that are not systematic average out over many queries. The reverse also holds: a small systematic bias can flip close systems even when kappa looks fine.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Task-specific eval sets, regression tests and significance
md: Report a gain as an interval, computed by resampling items with both systems paired. If the interval includes zero, say "not distinguishable on this set" and either add items or keep the old version. Check slices as well as the average.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
md: Model weights are paid once; KV is paid per token per sequence. A common mistake is to size a deployment by "the model fits on the GPU". A model that fits with 2 GB to spare can serve almost nobody: 2 GB is only about 15,000 tokens of Llama 3 8B's KV cache.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Few-shot examples and asking the model to reason first
md: Examples fix the *format*; reasoning before the answer improves the *content* on multi-step problems. Both work only through the context the model reads before it commits to a token.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Ambiguity, negation and graceful fallback
md: Never silently drop a filter the user asked for. A validator that deletes an unknown value and runs the rest turns *rust engineers in Gotham* into *rust engineers anywhere*, and the user believes the results are in Gotham.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
md: FIRST needs two things a plain chat API may not give you: logits over the identifier tokens at the first position, and a model whose first-token logits are trained or validated to rank well. With a zero-shot model, check that the logit order matches its generated order before trusting it.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Why sending every prompt to the strongest model wastes money
md: Routing pays off when two things are true at once: the price gap between models is large, and a sizable share of your prompts are ones where the weak model is just as good. If every prompt is hard, no router can save money without losing quality.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
md: Judge a match by how much better it is than the runner-up, not by its absolute distance. The ratio d1/d2 adapts to how distinctive each descriptor is.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: CAS compares bits, not history. Any lock-free algorithm that frees or reuses nodes must either version its pointers or guarantee that no thread can still hold a reference to a node that gets reused.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: From templates to counts, time series and alerts
md: Parsing accuracy is not the goal; downstream behaviour is. SHISO parsed 93 percent of messages into the right groups and still produced 7 times the false alarms, because the templates it got wrong were ones the detector was sensitive to. Always evaluate a parser change by re-running the task that consumes its output.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: With dynamic scaling the RoPE of every cached token changes when $s$ changes. The YaRN paper notes the correct implementation caches keys *before* applying RoPE; caching rotated keys silently mixes two different scalings.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: A looped transformer decouples depth from parameter count. $(k \otimes L)$ has $k$ layers of parameters and $kL$ layers of sequential computation.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA does not compress or approximate the pretrained weight. W0 keeps all its information at full rank. Only the *change* learned during fine-tuning is restricted to rank r.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
md: Near-chance accuracy on a multiple-choice proxy shows the model no longer *answers* those questions. It does not show the knowledge is gone from the weights. The WMDP authors say so themselves: because RMU edits only three layers it "perhaps obfuscates knowledge more than unlearns it", and in their appendix fine-tuning on the forget corpus recovered the performance.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: How rankings shift as you cut dimensions: Matryoshka vs standard
md: A good Matryoshka prefix gives a coarser version of the full ranking: close items blur together, but far items stay far. A standard model's prefix gives a different, noisy ranking. That is why Matryoshka prefixes are safe for shortlisting.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
md: Do not compare a paper's achieved TFLOP/s across systems without checking what it counts. Narayanan et al.'s 52% includes recomputation FLOPs; PaLM introduced MFU precisely because HFU depends on implementation choices like rematerialization.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production
md: Fix the layer the numbers point at. Slack inside pages (active over allocated) needs objects moved or lifetimes grouped. Unused resident pages (resident over active) need purging or decay. Missing high-order physical blocks need compaction. Reaching for the wrong tool spends CPU and changes nothing.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Why freeing a removed node is the hard part
md: A garbage collector does not make ABA impossible in every case. Michael points out that if a program moves the same live node back and forth between two lists, ABA can still occur even with perfect GC. What a GC (and the schemes in this course) guarantees is narrower: a node's address is not reused while someone can still reach it.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Grace periods (EBR, RCU) make reads cheap but let one stalled reader block all reclamation. Hazard pointers bound garbage at N x R but charge every visited node. Pick by read pattern and by how much you trust threads to keep moving.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
md: In-domain scores do not transfer. In the same paper, the full model trained on Market-1501 reaches only 27.5% rank-1 on DukeMTMC-reID, and random erasing, which helps in-domain, hurts cross-domain. New cameras, sites or seasons need their own evaluation.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Noise you can see and average away; bias you cannot. Vary the setup (layout, link order, process, machine) and trust only effects that survive the variation.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
md: Bitwise-equal logprobs do not make an async run on-policy. True-on-policy alignment removes numerical mismatch between engines, not staleness from training on groups generated under older weights; the data buffer bounds that separately.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
md: The paper counts cache size in **elements**, regardless of storage precision. Quantizing the cache to FP8 or lower is a separate, stackable trick. When comparing headline numbers, check whether both sides use the same precision.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
md: Merge when one adapter dominates the traffic and per-token latency matters most. Keep adapters unmerged when many adapters are active concurrently, so the base matmul can be batched across all of them.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
md: Asking for diversity cuts both ways. Raudaschl's repo has a diverse mode whose prompt asks for synonyms, broader or narrower framings and related sub-topics, and to avoid minor rewordings. That reduces redundancy but pushes phrasings toward the edge of the topic, where drift lives. Inspect generated queries on real traffic before tuning N.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: From one target per position to n targets per position
md: Multi-token prediction keeps the input and the causal context the same and only adds targets: each position is asked for tokens t+1 through t+n, all from the prefix ending at t.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
md: Muon does not produce an exactly orthogonal matrix. The reference implementation's docstring says the result is closer to $US'V^\top$ with the entries of $S'$ roughly uniform in $[0.5, 1.5]$, and that this does not hurt model performance. The Moonlight team also found 10 steps gave a more accurate result than 5 but no better training.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
md: Random weights times activations grow like sqrt(n); updates times activations grow like n, because updates are correlated with the activations they act on. muP sets each layer's init and learning rate so that both effects stay order 1.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
md: Returning from FUTEX_WAIT does not mean the lock is yours. The call can fail with EAGAIN, be interrupted by a signal (EINTR), or wake spuriously, and another thread may grab the lock first. Always loop and re-check the word.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
md: Read Committed: new snapshot per statement, writers re-apply on top of concurrent commits. Repeatable Read: one snapshot per transaction, writers that hit a concurrent commit get error 40001 and must retry.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The metric: entity-level micro F1 with exact span match
md: Never report token accuracy for NER. CoNLL-2003 English training data holds one entity per 8.7 tokens, so the great majority of tags are O and a tagger that predicts O everywhere scores high token accuracy with an entity F1 of exactly zero. Entity-level micro F1 is the metric; token accuracy is a training diagnostic at best.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
md: A perceptual hash is a summary you **compare**, not an identity you **look up**. Similar images give hashes at a small Hamming distance; the system decides a threshold for what counts as a match.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Training backends (Automodel, Megatron) and generation backends
md: Training parallelism and generation parallelism are separate settings. For example vLLM's `tensor_parallel_size` is unrelated to Megatron's `tensor_model_parallel_size`. Refit must reshape weights from the trainer's layout into the engine's layout, which is part of why refit transports matter (lesson 4).

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
md: Policy = mode + nodes + scope, applied at allocation time. Use bind for strict isolation, preferred when spilling over is acceptable, interleave for big shared data, and leave private per-thread data on the default local policy.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: What a detector outputs, and how two boxes are compared
md: A detector outputs a variable-size set of (box, class, score) triples, and IoU between boxes is the measure every later stage builds on.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Counting objects: by detection, by density, by tracking
md: Pick the counting method by scene: detection when objects are separable and you need locations, density maps for dense crowds where boxes fail, and tracking plus line or region events for video, where the same object appears in many frames.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Never compute a rate as last value minus first value over a counter. One restart in the window turns a positive rate into a large negative number, and `rate()` exists precisely to handle that case for you.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
md: OCR is a chain: detect, then recognize, then order and extract. Each stage only sees the previous stage's output, so an early error silently becomes a wrong field later.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
md: Rebuild cost is decided by the include graph. Touching a header recompiles every translation unit that reaches it, directly or transitively. That is why big projects keep widely included headers small and stable.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs
md: A red X on one matrix cell with grey cancelled cells next to it does not mean the other platforms passed. With fail-fast they never finished. Look at which job failed first; that is the one with the real log.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Answering review comments as the author
md: Never reply in anger. Google's guide calls it a serious breach of etiquette that lives forever in the review tool. If a comment stings, ask what constructive point the reviewer is making, and answer that point once you are calm.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Issue first: when to ask, how to report, how to claim work
md: Closing keywords (`close`, `closes`, `closed`, `fix`, `fixes`, `fixed`, `resolve`, `resolves`, `resolved`) only work when the PR targets the repository's **default branch**. Aimed at a release or feature branch, the keyword is ignored and the issue stays open after merge.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
md: Rebasing replays your commits on a new base. Every replayed commit gets a new hash because its parent changed, even if its diff is identical.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
md: A license is permission plus conditions. The conditions only apply when you do the thing they attach to, which for most licenses means distributing the code.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
md: A performance claim is an experiment. The PR must let a reviewer rerun it (exact commands, setup, commits) and weigh it (spread, significance and costs), not just read a headline number.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Search that narrows: git grep, ripgrep and word matches
md: GitHub's "find references" is name-based: the docs say it searches all definitions and references across a repository "to find entities with a given name". Two unrelated functions with the same name in different modules will both show up. Check the file and its imports before you trust a reference.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Delta debugging: let a script shrink the repro
md: Automated reduction needs only a yes or no oracle: does this candidate still show the exact failure? Write that test carefully and the tool does the tedious part.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
md: Each PR (and each commit in a series) should be justifiable on its own and leave the project building and passing tests. If one depends on another, say so in the description.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: Paging is not free. The paper measured 20 to 26% higher attention kernel latency than FasterTransformer's kernel, from block-table lookups, extra branches and variable lengths. It still wins end to end because only the attention operator pays, and the larger batch more than makes up for it.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: From perf.data to folded stacks
md: In `perf report`, a high Children value does not mean the function is doing the work. main is 100% in every program. Sort by Self to find what executes, by Children to find which caller to change.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
md: Visibility and durability are different events. A store becomes visible when it reaches the coherent cache, and durable only when its line reaches the persistence domain. On ADR platforms, software must close that gap explicitly.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
md: A top-down pose model inherits every mistake of its detector. If two people overlap and NMS merges their boxes, or the detector misses someone, the keypoint network has no way to recover that person. OpenPose's authors call this **early commitment**.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: Post-filtering leaves the index untouched and is cheap when $s$ is large, but the result count is a random variable. To hold k results you must fetch on the order of $k/s$ candidates, and noticeably more for a high-probability guarantee.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Hardware prefetchers: patterns, training and the page wall
md: Hardware prefetching is not free: every useless prefetch costs memory bandwidth and can evict a line you still needed. That is how it can make a random walk slower than raw memory latency. Drepper describes Intel's model-specific register switch for disabling it (bit 9 of IA32_MISC_ENABLE on many processors of that time) for workloads that measurably suffer.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
md: Do not judge a PRM only by best-of-N accuracy. That metric checks final answers, rewards PRMs that act like outcome models, and depends on which generator produced the samples. Check step-level error location (for example ProcessBench) on the distribution you will actually run it on.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Why billion-vector indexes need compressed codes
md: PQ builds an exponentially large codebook, $(k^*)^m$ centroids, out of $m$ tiny ones. Each vector costs $m \log_2 k^*$ bits no matter how many dimensions it has.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Managed prompt optimizers and a practical workflow
md: A rewrite produced without evaluation data is a hypothesis, not a result. Treat it like a candidate from a proposer: score it on your validation set against the current prompt before shipping.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym expansion on the toy corpus: recall up, precision at risk
md: Misconception: expansion always helps. It helps when the added words mean the same thing **in this query's context**. *auto* means automobile in d6 but automatic in d9; a list that ignores sense trades recall for false matches. Here the bad synonym cost nothing at the top only because the good documents happened to score higher.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
md: Sign bits only carry information if coordinates are spread around zero. Qdrant's docs say binary quantization needs a *centered distribution* of vector components. If every coordinate is positive, every bit is 1 and all vectors look identical; non-negative data such as SIFT image descriptors comes close to this. Lesson 2 measures this failure.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft leader election: terms, votes and randomized timeouts
md: `currentTerm`, `votedFor` and the log must reach stable storage *before* a server answers an RPC. If a server voted, crashed, and forgot its vote, it could vote again in the same term for a different candidate, and two leaders could be elected for one term.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Evaluating retrieval and generation separately
md: Read the metrics as a grid. Low context recall: a **retrieval** problem. High context recall but low faithfulness: a **generation** problem. High faithfulness but wrong answer: the context itself was wrong or stale, an **index** problem.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
md: **Recall@k is not Success@k.** Some papers report "Recall@k" meaning *at least one relevant document is in the top k*. The ir_measures documentation calls that **Success@k** and reserves R@k for the fraction of all relevant documents retrieved. For q1 every run has Success@5 = 1, while R@5 ranges from 0.167 to 0.667. Check which one a paper means before comparing numbers.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
md: An (address, rkey) pair is a capability: whoever holds it, on a QP in the same protection domain, can read or write that memory with no further check by your CPU. Grant the narrowest access flags you need, and revoke by deregistering (`ibv_dereg_mr`) or with memory windows, which the manual describes as a cheaper way to grant and revoke remote access dynamically.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Client-side prediction and server reconciliation
md: Each server state is a statement about the past: "here is the world after your input #n". Reset to it, then replay inputs after #n. Sequence numbers are what make that subtraction possible.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
md: Implicit feedback = preference (did it happen) x confidence (how sure we are). The confidence weights decide which events the factors must explain.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Rectifying the plane: card corners to millimeters
md: Map the object's **points** into plane millimeters first, then measure there. Never measure in pixels and convert with a scalar; the homography's division by w is where perspective gets removed.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
md: Synchronous does not mean "followers are always up to date for reads". With `synchronous_commit = on` the standby has *flushed* the record but may not have *replayed* it yet, so a query on that standby can still miss it. Only `remote_apply` waits until the change is visible on the standby, and the docs warn it causes much larger commit delays.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Goodhart measured: gold reward rises, then falls
md: Misconception: overoptimization is a fixed point you either cross or not. The curve is smooth. Gold reward usually *improves* first, which is why a rising training reward looks like success. You only see the turn if you evaluate with something other than the reward you train on.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: After new weights land, cached KV entries are wrong: they were computed by the old weights. SGLang's `update_weights_from_distributed` flushes the cache by default, and AReaL's interruptible workers discard KV caches and recompute them with the new weights before continuing unfinished sequences.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: One fault, 397 alerts: collapsing the storm
md: Dedup and grouping are lossless: they change how many notifications you receive, not what was observed. Inhibition and silences are lossy: they delete evidence from your view. Use the first two freely and the last two sparingly.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: Do not confuse RRF's k with the k of k-nearest-neighbors. Azure AI Search's docs stress that the RRF constant is "entirely separate" from the k that sets how many neighbors a vector query returns. Elasticsearch names them `rank_constant` and `rank_window_size` to avoid the clash.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
md: The pattern is always the same: an `unsafe` C protocol (lock and unlock, get and put, register and unregister) becomes a value whose constructor does the first half and whose `Drop` does the second. The type system then tracks the protocol for every caller.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
md: Weighted fairness in sched_ext can be three lines: order a custom DSQ by vtime, charge `used x 100 / weight` in `stopping`, and cap how far behind a waking task's vtime may be. Everything else (CPU placement, preemption, latency boosts) is extra policy you choose to add.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs
md: SPIN's fixed point is the human data distribution. It can extract more from an SFT dataset than plain SFT does, but it cannot surpass that data: once the model's responses are indistinguishable from the human ones, the loss gives no signal.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
md: Evaluate compression like a model change: measure your task metric at several ratios on your own data, and measure end-to-end latency including the compressor. The published gains were measured on specific benchmarks with specific target models.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
md: Prefix reuse is a property of the *whole serving path*: frontend hints, the radix tree, queue order on each worker, and routing across workers. Each layer can preserve reuse or destroy it.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
md: Production routing = a graph from OSM (directed, with turn costs) + a preprocessing technique. CH gives the fastest queries on a fixed metric; partition-based MLD or CRP accepts new weights in seconds without redoing the expensive phase.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Why speedups fall short: latency chains and the memory wall
md: Two ceilings limit SIMD: latency chains (fix with several independent accumulators) and memory bandwidth (fix by doing more work per byte or keeping data in cache). Lane count only matters once both are out of the way.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
md: Bump allocation costs a few instructions and has no per-object free. It is ideal when a group of objects share one lifetime (a request, a frame, a compiler pass) and wrong when objects die at unrelated times, because one long-lived object keeps the whole arena alive.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
md: The colocated code keeps a comment worth remembering: SGLang returns from the update request after enqueueing GPU copies, not after they finish. Reusing the same flattened IPC buffer for the next bucket right away could overwrite memory SGLang is still reading and corrupt weights, so slime allocates a fresh buffer per bucket.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
md: L1 penalises size, so it shrinks every active latent. TopK (fixed k), Gated (separate gate) and JumpReLU (learned per-latent thresholds with an L0 penalty) all separate deciding which latents fire from estimating how big they are.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Inverse distance weighting: weights from distance alone
md: IDW ignores how sensors sit relative to each other. S1 and S2 are only 2.24 km apart and both read 11, so they carry nearly the same information. IDW still counts both at full weight. If ten sensors sat in one parking lot, IDW would let that lot outvote everything else. Kriging, later in the course, fixes this.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap
md: Decoding is slow because each step moves all the weights to produce one token. Checking $K$ guessed tokens in one target pass moves the weights once, so every accepted guess is a target step you did not pay for.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
md: Mel settings are not interchangeable. librosa defaults to the Slaney scale, while `torchaudio.transforms.MelSpectrogram` defaults to `mel_scale='htk'` and `n_mels=128`. Features computed with different settings than a model was trained on look like a different microphone to the model.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
md: `free` rarely shrinks your process. Freed small chunks go back on glibc's free lists, not to the kernel, and a single live chunk near the top of the heap blocks trimming. A process whose memory never drops after a burst is usually not leaking; check whether the memory is reusable before hunting leaks.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
md: A steering vector edits **activations**, not weights and not the prompt. It is computed once, before inference, and the same vector is added on every forward pass while it is switched on.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
md: Two different knobs, often confused. The bound $B$ moves the watermark (how long to wait before the first result). The allowed lateness $L$ keeps state after that (how long to accept corrections). Raising $B$ delays every result; raising $L$ costs state memory and extra firings but does not delay the first result.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
md: Attention output for a position = softmax(its query dotted with every key, divided by the square root of d_k), used as weights on the value vectors. Every step is a matrix multiply or a row-wise softmax, so all positions are computed at once.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
md: Length normalization is relative to avgdl, so only a document's length compared with the average matters. An average-length document scores the same for every b.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
md: A GPT is just: embed (token + position), $L$ x [pre-LN causal attention, pre-LN MLP, each added to the residual stream], final LayerNorm, project back to vocabulary scores with the tied embedding matrix.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
md: Chain rule: the derivative of a pipeline is the **product of the local derivatives** of its stages, each evaluated at the value that stage actually saw. Backpropagation is this rule applied systematically.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
md: Quote every expansion (`"$f"`, `"$(cmd)"`, `"$@"`) unless you specifically want splitting and globbing. Unquoted is the exception you choose, not the default.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
md: Vector arithmetic analogies are a nice demo, not a law. The answer depends on excluding inputs, and Nissim et al. show that other implementation choices (casing, frequency cutoffs, the exact formula) change results too. The same arithmetic surfaces social biases: Bolukbasi et al. (2016) found that the GoogleNews word2vec vectors complete *man : computer programmer :: woman : x* with *homemaker*.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token
md: Reserving the maximum length for every request wastes most of the cache. vLLM's profiling found only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV memory held actual token states in earlier systems, due to reserved slots and fragmentation. PagedAttention fixes this by allocating the cache in small fixed-size blocks, like OS pages.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
md: `call` = push return address + jump. `ret` = pop into the program counter. Everything a function keeps on the stack lives only until it returns, which is why the stack can be reused so cheaply.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Supervised fine-tuning: same loss, curated data, masked prompt
md: SFT does not add much new knowledge. If the base model does not know a fact, a demonstration that states it mostly teaches the model to answer confidently in that style, which can increase made-up answers on other questions ([Gekhman et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05904)).

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Building the index: tokens, sorting and postings
md: Whatever normalization you apply at index time (lowercasing, stemming, stripping punctuation) you must apply identically to queries. If the index stores `cache` and the query parser passes `Cache` through unchanged, the dictionary lookup finds nothing.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
md: A header declaring a function is not the same as the function existing. `#include` only pastes a promise into your file. If the definition lives in `area.c` (or a library), it must also reach the linker, or the build fails at link time with an undefined symbol error even though every file compiled cleanly.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
md: 'It runs fine' is not evidence that C code is correct. A clean run without sanitizers says almost nothing about memory safety; even a clean sanitizer run covers only the paths your inputs exercised.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs
md: Lifetime annotations do not change how long anything lives. They describe relationships between references so the borrow checker can verify each call site. The function body is checked against the signature, and callers are checked against the signature alone.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
md: $A\mathbf{x}$ is both a stack of dot products (one per row) and a weighted sum of columns. The columns of $A$ are the images of the basis vectors, so they fully describe the map.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Mini-batches, cross-entropy gradients and the training loop
md: SGD steps on an unbiased but noisy gradient estimate from a minibatch. Noise falls only as $1/\sqrt B$, so moderate batches with many steps are usually the efficient choice.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The chain rule on a computational graph
md: Backprop = for each node in reverse order: upstream gradient times local gradient, summed over every path that leaves the node. One backward sweep yields the gradient for every input at once.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
md: "It is a single line of C" does not make it atomic, and `volatile` does not either. OSTEP's counter is declared `volatile int` and still loses updates.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Why averages are stable: the law of large numbers and the CLT
md: The CLT needs independent samples and a finite variance. Correlated samples (consecutive tokens, users who appear many times) have a larger true standard error than $\sigma/\sqrt n$. Very heavy-tailed data converges slowly, and for distributions like the Cauchy, which has no mean, the average never settles at all.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
md: Compute-optimal training scales model size and data **together**, each roughly as the square root of compute. The rule of thumb that falls out is about 20 training tokens per parameter.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Graded relevance and nDCG: rewarding the best result first
md: IDCG must come from **all** judged documents in the qrels, not from re-sorting the documents your run retrieved. Re-sorting only the retrieved ones gives IDCG 5.193 and nDCG@10 = 0.674 instead of 0.576, and hides the fact that the run missed d9 entirely. trec_eval builds the ideal from the qrels.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
md: Contrastive training with in-batch negatives is what turns a language model into an embedding model: pull each true pair together, push everything else in the batch apart, with a scale (temperature) that controls how sharply.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Byte-level BPE: how GPT-2 and its successors tokenize anything
md: Byte-level BPE = UTF-8 bytes as the base alphabet (256 symbols, so nothing is ever unknown) + a regex pre-tokenizer that limits where merges can happen + an ordered merge list. Decoding concatenates bytes and is lossless.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
md: ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude fewer distance computations. Every ANN number you read (or report) should come as a pair: recall@k and speed, measured against exact brute-force results on the same queries.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: The Gaussian loop: unbiased fits that still shrink to a point
md: Sampling error makes each generation's fit a random step, and steps that multiply variance by a mean-one factor still shrink it in the typical run. Unbiased estimation does not save a closed loop.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: A system call is a mode switch plus cache pollution, paid per call. Make fewer, bigger calls (buffering, vectored I/O, batching) and let the vDSO serve the hottest read-only queries without entering the kernel.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Measuring correctly: intended start times and HdrHistogram
md: Latency = completion time minus *intended* start time. The intended start comes from a load plan that does not depend on how fast the server answers.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
md: Derived numbers go stale. *Years of experience* computed at index time is wrong a month later for everyone with a current role. Store intervals with open ends and compute tenure at query time against the query's reference date, or recompute on a schedule and record the as-of date.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
md: Thinking longer does not scale forever. s1's gains flattened after about six forced continuations, suppressing the stop too often led to repetitive loops, and the context window caps how long one trace can be. Parallel methods (voting, PRM search over several traces) can extend scaling past that point; s1 found they complement sequential scaling.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Wiring learned memory into real models, and what it costs
md: Common failure modes: (1) Wall-clock, not FLOPs, is the bottleneck. The TTT paper reports that TTT-MLP still faces challenges in memory I/O, and Titans' throughput falls roughly linearly with memory depth. (2) Inner learning rates that are too large make the memory diverge (lesson 2). (3) Without forgetting, a fixed-size memory overflows on long inputs. (4) Most published comparisons use models under 1.5B parameters.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
md: Tiers are not the same as NUMA distance. A remote-socket DRAM node is far, but it has CPUs and DRAM-class performance, so it sits in the top tier and is never a demotion target for the other socket. Only slower memory types form lower tiers.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Honest evaluation: error metrics, MASE and rolling origins
md: Report a forecast's accuracy as an average over many origins, at the horizon you will use in production, with a scaled metric such as MASE next to seasonal naive. A single train/test split can rank two methods either way by luck.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
md: Triton moves the hard parts of a CUDA kernel (coalescing, shared memory, barriers, pipelining) into the compiler, and leaves you the decisions that need knowledge of the problem: the tiling, the program-to-tile order, the masks, and a short list of configs to autotune.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
md: A unikernel is **one application plus only the OS code it uses, linked into one image that boots directly on a hypervisor**. The hypervisor, not a guest kernel, is the isolation boundary.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
md: A common mistake is to benchmark a distance kernel on a few thousand vectors that fit in L2 cache and extrapolate to a 100 GB index. The small benchmark measures compute; the real index measures memory.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Why verl splits the RL loop from the GPU programs
md: The controller decides **what runs and in what order**; each WorkerGroup decides **how** it runs on its GPUs. That is why a new algorithm is a change to one Python loop, and a new backend or placement is a change to the workers or the config, never both.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Why an hour of video does not fit: frames times tokens
